en.title: You might not need an agent at all
en.summary: Many teams hand a batch of repetitive tasks to an Agent and let it plan on its own, call tools, and make judgment calls over and over. It looks smart in a demo, but in real-world use it's slow, expensive, inconsistent from run to run, and hard to reproduce when something goes wrong. The author offers a more pragmatic routing approach for anyone building AI automation: decide first which tasks should go to whom, and both cost and stability become far more manageable.
en.reason: Parcha's agent failed at real customer deployments, while Jev and Parallel decision models can complete a one-page image Q&A or web search in half a second for roughly one-tenth of a cent, so rules should stay in code.

en.title: 3 Ways to Improve Agents: Simulation, Trajectories, and Evaluation
en.summary: Once an Agent ships, it's easy to fall into a loop: a user reports an error, you tweak the Prompt, it feels fixed, and two days later it breaks in a different scenario. The real problem is that teams only have scattered feedback and no mechanism for turning failures into improvements. In this article, the author shares three complementary approaches to iteration that may help.
en.reason: Ashpreet Bedi uses a daily briefing agent to show how simulation, traces and sessions, and evaluation complement each other, with Agno’s /improve skill letting coding agents recursively optimize agents under real model calls and tool execution.

en.title: When CI breaks, who's the gatekeeper? Buildkite's new agent approach
en.summary:
Buildkite adds scoped secrets and agent CI tools

Buildkite has introduced pipeline-scoped secrets and MCP tools, strengthening secret isolation and build observability; it also added Linux arm64 support for its GitHub Actions compatibility layer and enhanced the Agent's OpenTelemetry data collection and sensitive-information redaction.

Secrets can be scoped to a single pipeline and authorized dynamically by branch, queue, source, and creator; the MCP tools support pipeline validation, failure diagnosis, and webhook remediation; the CLI provides a GitHub Actions secret migration command and path compatibility fixes.

Intended for DevOps engineers, SREs, and CI/CD platform developers.

Continuous integration provider Buildkite has launched pipeline-scoped secrets and new Model Context Protocol (MCP) tools for validating pipelines, diagnosing build failures, and fixing webhooks. The company also added Linux arm64 support to its GitHub Actions compatibility layer and expanded OpenTelemetry support in Buildkite Agent v4.1.0.
en.reason: Buildkite now scopes secrets to a single pipeline with authorization by branch, queue, source or creator, and ships MCP tools such as validate_pipeline and compare_builds so agents can check YAML, diagnose failed builds and repair webhooks.

en.title: ChatGPT Pro doubles its quota: a concession, not a perk?
en.summary:
Agents burn tokens in overlooked places
Agents burn tokens in overlooked places
Word count: 4,379 · Reading time: ~14 minutes
OpenAI announced that usage quotas across all Pro and Business Premium tiers are doubling, confirming that Pro 200 keeps its existing ChatGPT Work and Codex allocations while Dots quota remains calculated separately. The move is a direct response to user feedback, reversing a previously planned cut to Pro 200 quotas. Pro 500 users get roughly 50x the usage of the Plus plan, widening the gap between tiers.
Pro 200 users gain no real increase in benefits — only the avoidance of a cut; Dots quota is fully isolated from the main account; Pro 500 cements its position as the high-end option for intensive AI workflows.
Intended for AI platform product managers, enterprise SaaS architects, and developer-tool procurement decision-makers.
On October 29, OpenAI product lead Tibo announced that starting immediately, usage limits for the Pro 100, Pro 200, Pro 500, and Business Premium plans are all doubling.
One important note: after listening to user feedback, OpenAI decided not to cut Pro 200 usage quotas, so ChatGPT Work and Codex usage on that plan will stay at current levels.
en.reason: OpenAI doubled usage limits across Pro 100, Pro 200, Pro 500 and Business Premium on October 29, but Pro 200 users only kept existing ChatGPT Work and Codex quotas—no real gain—while Pro 500 now gets roughly 50x Plus usage.

en.title: Baidu Search AI API costs just RMB 4.9 per 1,000 calls, undercutting DeepSeek; search has entered the RSI era
en.summary:
Baidu officially launches AI interactive drama and AI interactive apps

Word count: 2,235
Reading time: about 7 minutes

Baidu has upgraded its search AI API, launching an enhanced version at RMB 4.9 per thousand calls — below DeepSeek's pricing — to deepen its reach into Agent scenarios. Built on a four-layer AI-native architecture, it lifts content trustworthiness by more than 50%, drives model iteration through a closed online feedback loop, and enables multi-Agent collaborative self-evolution.

The pricing strategy lowers the barrier to Agent calls; the content layer combines a hundred-billion-scale index with LLM judgment for a marked improvement in trustworthiness; the engine layer supports recursive "retrieval–feedback–retraining" optimization.

Intended for search architects, Agent developers, and heads of enterprise AI platforms.

On October 30, Baidu APP rolled out a series of upgrades spanning the search box, AI camera, GUI visualization, and AI interactive apps, alongside a fully upgraded search AI API. On pricing, the enhanced search AI API is available for as low as RMB 4.9 per thousand calls during the promotional period, with the flagship version at RMB 9.9 per thousand calls. Baidu says the RMB 4.9 rate is lower than DeepSeek's search API, and it hopes to expand the use of its search capabilities in Agents through lower call costs.

At the same time, Baidu is further opening up multiple access methods including API, MCP, and Skill, hoping to release search capabilities from within Baidu APP to more A

en.title: AI code review recall tested: caught 13 of 20 mutants that fooled unit tests
en.summary:
AI Code Review Recall Test: 13 of 20 Mutants That Fooled Unit Tests Caught

The previous post covered AI code review precision: 1,919 lines of Java, 18 issues flagged, 8 true, 8 false, 2 pending—50% precision.

That post only answered “how accurate are the flags?” This one answers another question: **does it miss things?**

The method isn’t “get a few people to review it and share their impressions.” It’s injecting known defects, having the model review blind, and counting hits. Below is the full breakdown of the design, results, causes of missed detections, and cost. The method is reproducible.

- Injected 23 mutants; 3 were caught by existing unit tests and eliminated; **20 entered the blind test**
- Concurrency **4/4 caught**; security 3/4; null values, exceptions, and resources 2/4 each
- Of the 7 missed, 5 were “remove or replace one defensive step”
- 20 blind runs used ~1.65 million tokens, 50k–154k per run

The ideal corpus is production incidents and human review records. Unavailable: the project is a personal one, all 25 commits were made by me, there were no review comments, and therefore no ground truth.

en.reason: Blind-review testing of 20 mutants that escaped existing unit tests caught 13, with concurrency defects at 4/4 and 5 of the 7 misses involving a deleted or swapped defensive step, at a disclosed cost of 50,000–154,000 tokens per run.

市面上的健康管理 App 要么功能太重（会员、社交、广告），要么我不敢把全家人的医疗影像传给一个我不了解的服务器。于是决定自己写一个「电子病例夹」：

en.title: I built a medical records archiving mini-program and got a harsh lesson in the "last mile" of AI recognition
en.summary:
I Built a Medical Records Mini Program, and AI Recognition's "Last Mile" Taught Me a Hard Lesson

Anyone with kids knows the drill: medical record books, lab reports, discharge summaries, vaccination booklets... scattered across bags. Next time you go for a follow-up and want to find "which hospital ran that blood panel two visits ago," you're digging through everything for ten minutes.

Health management apps on the market are either too heavy (memberships, social features, ads), or I don't dare upload my whole family's medical imaging to a server I know nothing about. So I decided to write my own "electronic medical record folder":

*   **Frontend**: native WeChat Mini Program, four pages (Home / Photo Capture / Detail / Profile)
*   **Backend**: pure Node.js built-in modules, just run `node index.js`, **zero third-party dependencies**
*   **AI recognition**: after taking a photo, automatically extract "visit date / hospital / disease name / report category," with hot-switching across three engines

The whole project is under 30 files, yet it walked me through the questions I get asked most often about shipping AI applications in 2026:

1.  Running a local vision LLM takes 40–60 seconds per inference, but `wx.request` caps timeouts at 60 seconds — what do you do?
en.reason: A WeChat mini-program for archiving medical records pairs a native frontend with a zero-dependency Node.js backend, and its local Ollama Qwen2.5-VL 3B recognition takes 40–60 seconds per image, forcing async tasks plus 1.2-second polling under wx.request’s 60-second limit.

Title: 我把 0.6B 大模型塞进安卓手机：596 秒到 10 秒
Published Time: 2026-10-31T07:24:24+00:00
我做了一个自动记账的 App，它可以读一张支付截图，认出金额、商户和日期，自动记成一笔账，全程不联网。
里面是端侧 OCR 加 0.6B 的小模型，全部跑在手机本地。
这 60 倍里，没有一倍是花在模型上的。
| 基线 | llama.cpp，Q8_0，ARM 默认编译 | 596 秒 |

| 三 | 切 OpenCL GPU，补采样器 | 17.4 秒 |
| 四 | 输出契约砍到 4 字段，引擎常驻 | 8.4 到 11 秒 |
质量闸门全程 30/30 通过，金额识别 96.7%，日期 100%。
596 秒是什么感觉，用户拍完照泡了杯茶回来，还在转圈。
这不是慢一点，是根本不能用。所以我后面所有的工作，都不是性能调优，是让这个东西能存在。

en.title: You might not need an agent at all
en.summary: Many teams hand a batch of repetitive tasks to an Agent and let it plan on its own, call tools, and make judgment calls over and over. It looks smart in a demo, but in real-world use it's slow, expensive, inconsistent from run to run, and hard to reproduce when something goes wrong. The author offers a more pragmatic routing approach for anyone building AI automation: decide first which tasks should go to whom, and both cost and stability become far more manageable.
en.reason: Parcha's agent failed at real customer deployments, while Jev and Parallel decision models can complete a one-page image Q&A or web search in half a second for roughly one-tenth of a cent, so rules should stay in code.

en.title: 3 Ways to Improve Agents: Simulation, Trajectories, and Evaluation
en.summary: Once an Agent ships, it's easy to fall into a loop: a user reports an error, you tweak the Prompt, it feels fixed, and two days later it breaks in a different scenario. The real problem is that teams only have scattered feedback and no mechanism for turning failures into improvements. In this article, the author shares three complementary approaches to iteration that may help.

en.title: When CI breaks, who's the gatekeeper? Buildkite's new agent approach
en.summary:
Buildkite adds scoped secrets and agent CI tools

Buildkite has introduced pipeline-scoped secrets and MCP tools, strengthening secret isolation and build observability; it also added Linux arm64 support for its GitHub Actions compatibility layer and enhanced the Agent's OpenTelemetry data collection and sensitive-information redaction.

Secrets can be scoped to a single pipeline and authorized dynamically by branch, queue, source, and creator; the MCP tools support pipeline validation, failure diagnosis, and webhook remediation; the CLI provides a GitHub Actions secret migration command and path compatibility fixes.

Intended for DevOps engineers, SREs, and CI/CD platform developers.

Continuous integration provider Buildkite has launched pipeline-scoped secrets and new Model Context Protocol (MCP) tools for validating pipelines, diagnosing build failures, and fixing webhooks. The company also added Linux arm64 support to its GitHub Actions compatibility layer and expanded OpenTelemetry support in Buildkite Agent v4.1.0.
en.reason: Buildkite now scopes secrets to a single pipeline with authorization by branch, queue, source or creator, and ships MCP tools such as validate_pipeline and compare_builds so agents can check YAML, diagnose failed builds and repair webhooks.

Agents burn tokens in overlooked places

OpenAI announced that usage quotas across all Pro and Business Premium tiers are doubling, confirming that Pro 200 keeps its existing ChatGPT Work and Codex allocations while Dots quota remains calculated separately. The move is a direct response to user feedback, reversing a previously planned cut to Pro 200 quotas. Pro 500 users get roughly 50x the usage of the Plus plan, widening the gap between tiers.
Pro 200 users gain no real increase in benefits — only the avoidance of a cut; Dots quota is fully isolated from the main account; Pro 500 cements its position as the high-end option for intensive AI workflows.

en.title: Baidu Search AI API costs just RMB 4.9 per 1,000 calls, undercutting DeepSeek; search has entered the RSI era
en.summary:
Baidu officially launches AI interactive drama and AI interactive apps

Word count: 2,235
Reading time: about 7 minutes

Baidu has upgraded its search AI API, launching an enhanced version at RMB 4.9 per thousand calls — below DeepSeek's pricing — to deepen its reach into Agent scenarios. Built on a four-layer AI-native architecture, it lifts content trustworthiness by more than 50%, drives model iteration through a closed online feedback loop, and enables multi-Agent collaborative self-evolution.

The pricing strategy lowers the barrier to Agent calls; the content layer combines a hundred-billion-scale index with LLM judgment for a marked improvement in trustworthiness; the engine layer supports recursive "retrieval–feedback–retraining" optimization.

Intended for search architects, Agent developers, and heads of enterprise AI platforms.

On October 30, Baidu APP rolled out a series of upgrades spanning the search box, AI camera, GUI visualization, and AI interactive apps, alongside a fully upgraded search AI API. On pricing, the enhanced search AI API is available for as low as RMB 4.9 per thousand calls during the promotional period, with the flagship version at RMB 9.9 per thousand calls. Baidu says the RMB 4.9 rate is lower than DeepSeek's search API, and it hopes to expand the use of its search capabilities in Agents through lower call costs.

At the same time, Baidu is further opening up multiple access methods including API, MCP, and Skill, hoping to release search capabilities from within Baidu APP to more A

en.title: AI code review recall tested: caught 13 of 20 mutants that fooled unit tests
en.summary:
AI Code Review Recall Test: 13 of 20 Mutants That Fooled Unit Tests Caught

The previous post covered AI code review precision: 1,919 lines of Java, 18 issues flagged, 8 true, 8 false, 2 pending—50% precision.

That post only answered “how accurate are the flags?” This one answers another question: **does it miss things?**

The method isn’t “get a few people to review it and share their impressions.” It’s injecting known defects, having the model review blind, and counting hits. Below is the full breakdown of the design, results, causes of missed detections, and cost. The method is reproducible.

- Injected 23 mutants; 3 were caught by existing unit tests and eliminated; **20 entered the blind test**
- Concurrency **4/4 caught**; security 3/4; null values, exceptions, and resources 2/4 each
- Of the 7 missed, 5 were “remove or replace one defensive step”
- 20 blind runs used ~1.65 million tokens, 50k–154k per run

The ideal corpus is production incidents and human review records. Unavailable: the project is a personal one, all 25 commits were made by me, there were no review comments, and therefore no ground truth.

As a fallback, use mutation testing (mutation...
en.reason: Blind-review testing of 20 mutants that escaped existing unit tests caught 13, with concurrency defects at 4/4 and 5 of the 7 misses involving a deleted or swapped defensive step, at a disclosed cost of 50,000–154,000 tokens per run.

en.title: I built a medical records archiving mini-program and got a harsh lesson in the "last mile" of AI recognition
en.summary:
I Built a Medical Records Mini Program, and AI Recognition's "Last Mile" Taught Me a Hard Lesson

Anyone with kids knows the drill: medical record books, lab reports, discharge summaries, vaccination booklets... scattered across bags. Next time you go for a follow-up and want to find "which hospital ran that blood panel two visits ago," you're digging through everything for ten minutes.

Health management apps on the market are either too heavy (memberships, social features, ads), or I don't dare upload my whole family's medical imaging to a server I know nothing about. So I decided to write my own "electronic medical record folder":

*   **Frontend**: native WeChat Mini Program, four pages (Home / Photo Capture / Detail / Profile)
*   **Backend**: pure Node.js built-in modules, just run `node index.js`, **zero third-party dependencies**
*   **AI recognition**: after taking a photo, automatically extract "visit date / hospital / disease name / report category," with hot-switching across three engines

The whole project is under 30 files, yet it walked me through the questions I get asked most often about shipping AI applications in 2026:

1.  Running a local vision LLM takes 40–60 seconds per inference, but `wx.request` caps timeouts at 60 seconds — what do you do?
en.reason: A WeChat mini-program for archiving medical records pairs a native frontend with a zero-dependency Node.js backend, and its local Ollama Qwen2.5-VL 3B recognition takes 40–60 seconds per image, forcing async tasks plus 1.2-second polling under wx.request’s 60-second limit.
